3288.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the ROOT (on the root itself when monosyllabic); the domain is the root/stem, not the surface word: aspect/plural prefixes and pronominal suffixes/enclitics are outside the domain and never move it, so the surface position varies (CHAGW-be• word-penult, ches-AGW-be• word-penult, cheseBE• word-final). In compounds the second root takes main stress; many adverbial suffixes behave like a second compound stem and take main stress (chagw-ŽAT). Spanish loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable.
3288.srule: Not mentioned in Long & Cruz 2000 [1999], Gramática zapoteca §0.4 'El acento' p. 407 (whole section read; only 'acento principal' = main stress is named, on the second root of compounds and on stress-taking adverbial suffixes; no non-primary stress is described). 3289.dq: The word, whether major or minor, is the unit of stress placement.
3289.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and derived from tone: within the phonological word (major = noun/verb root; minor = bound word), the syllable bearing the highest tone (H > M > L) is stressed; if two or more syllables tie for the highest tone, the first (leftmost) of them is stressed. No tone-independent positional or weight-based default is given.
3289.srule: Not mentioned in Haller 1980 (Section 8 'The phonological word', p.76, the book's only stress passage; Sections 7-9 read): a single tone-determined word stress is described and nothing is said about secondary or rhythmic stress.
3289.quote: The phonological word is closely related to grammatical word classes and can be devided into major and minor phonological words. Major phonological words correspond to noun and verb roots. The word, whether major or minor, is the unit of stress placement. The distribution of stress is conditioned by 1. tone - the syllable with the highest tone bears stress; 2. position - if several syllables bear the same tone and no other tone in the word is higher, then stress falls on the first of these syllables. ... Major phonological words are further marked by potential pause, while minor phonological …
3289.loc: Section 8 'The phonological word', p.76; tone inventory Section 7.1 'Contrastive tone', p.68; Section 3.4 'Tone', p.6.
3289.idn: Haller 1980 describes the Zulgo dialect (fieldwork 1976/77 at Tala-Zulgo; assistants speak 'the Zulgo dialect as it is represented there'), one of the three dialects Zulgo, Mineo, Gemjek he recognizes; the tone-driven stress rule is thus attested first-hand for Zulgo proper, not for Gemzek.
3289.tone: Three contrastive level tones (high, mid, low) on every syllable (sec. 7.1, p.68: 'Each syllable carries one of three contrastive level tones'; sec. 3.4 'Tone', p.6: 'Every syllable manifests one of three contrastive tones'); perturbations are single-syllable assimilation/dissimilation (7.2) and utterance-level downstep (7.3). Stress is a word-level prominence wholly predictable from tone: highest-toned syllable, leftmost on ties (sec. 8, p.76). Grep of the PDF and the IA scan: the only stress/accent/prominence hits are the four lines of sec. 8, so sec. 8 is the whole stress statement.

3290.tone: Røsok 2016 analyses Aari as a tone language with two tones H and L, syllable as TBU, contour tones (LH) on final syllables, OCP effects, and different tonal behaviour on nouns (root tones spread onto suffixes) vs verbs (suffix tones constant, root tones change by paradigm). She rejects Hayward's (1990) accent analysis (one H per word) because she finds words with several H tones and contour tones. Her only remarks on stress are generic (p. 87: in tone languages 'no distinction is made regarding what syllable in the word is pronounced with or without stress'; a H syllable may be perceived as more prominent) and she makes no first-hand claim about stress in Aari. Hayward 1990 (carried via Røsok pp. 26-27, 87-88, 107) called Aari an accent language: one high-pitched syllable per word, usually final in nouns, with exceptions; accent lexical in nouns and grammatical in verbs.

3305.qtr: The accent is a high-low (pitch) accent, as in Japanese. But it differs in character from the Japanese accent. In Japanese the important point is up to where the pitch is high and from where it becomes low, whereas in Ainu the point is up to where it is low and from where it becomes high. The place where it rises is fixed for each word; everything before it is low, and after it, unless it is raised by intonation, it usually becomes gradually lower. 3305.heavy: Closed syllable (閉音節, syllable ending in one of p, t, k, s, r, m, n, w, y) versus open syllable (開音節). Section ⑴ of the same appendix states that Hokkaido Ainu has no phonemic vowel-length distinction (北海道アイヌ語では、母音の長短の音韻的区別はない), so coda closure is the only weight criterion; accented vowels may be phonetically lengthened.
3305.dflt: Second syllable: when the first syllable is open the rise falls on σ2 regardless of the shape of later syllables (sapá 'head', ku=sápaha 'my head').
3305.prule: One low-to-high pitch rise per word, its position set by the shape of the first syllable: if the first syllable is closed (閉音節, CVC) the first syllable is high (sínrit, k=óyra); if the first syllable is open (開音節, CV) the pitch rises from the second syllable (sapá, ku=sápaha). Everything before the rise is low; after it the pitch falls gradually unless sentence intonation raises it. Stated as a 'marked tendency' (著しい傾向) of the Saru dialect; words that deviate are lexically marked with an acute in the dictionary (húci, k=étuhu, a=akíhi, ecioká).
3305.srule: Not mentioned in Tamura 1996 (Saru dialect dictionary, appendix 「アイヌ語沙流方言略説」 §1 音韻 ③アクセント and ④イントネーション, read in full): the source describes one low-to-high pitch rise per word and no secondary or rhythmic prominence.
3305.quote: アクセントは日本語と同じように高低アクセントである。しかし日本語のアクセントとは性格が違う。日本語では、どこまでが高く、どこからが低くなるかが重要なポイントであるが、アイヌ語では、どこまでが低く、どこから高くなるかがポイントである。語によって上昇するところがきまっており、それより前はすべて低く、それよりあとは抑揚（イントネーション）によって上がったりしなければ、だんだん低くなることが多い。 アクセントは地方によって違うが、沙流方言では、低から高へ上がる位置に関して著しい傾向がある。すなわち 第一音節が開音節ならば第二音節から高くなる。 sapá サパ 頭 ku=sápaha クサパハ 私の頭 第一音節が閉音節ならば第一音節が高い。 sínrit シンリッ 先祖 k=óyra コイラ 私は忘れた 表記上は、この傾向に合っているときは「´」をつけずにsapa, ku=sapaha, sinrit, k=oyraのように書き、この傾向に合わないとき（例外的なとき）のみ、アクセント記号を母音字の上につけて示す。 húci フチ おばあちゃん k=étuhu ケトゥフ 私の鼻 a=akíhi アアキヒ （引用文中で）私の弟 ecioká エチオカ あなたたち

3305.tone: The source labels the system 高低アクセント 'high-low (pitch) accent, as in Japanese' but notes it is of a different character: what is distinctive is where the pitch rises from low to high (Japanese: where it falls). Realization is pitch, not intensity; ⑴ 音素 adds that vowels may be lengthened by accent or intonation. No intensity stress is described. Verdict placed at weight-sensitive, stated with hedges because the source gives a weight-conditioned placement rule; an adjudicator who restricts QS codes to stress-accent systems would file it as tone or pitch accent with the same placement rule in this field.

tn.quote: アクセントは日本語と同じように高低アクセントである。しかし日本語のアクセントとは性格が違う。日本語では、どこまでが高く、どこからが低くなるかが重要なポイントであるが、アイヌ語では、どこまでが低く、どこから高くなるかがポイントである。語によって上昇するところがきまっており、それより前はすべて低く、それよりあとは抑揚（イントネーション）によって上がったりしなければ、だんだん低くなることが多い。 アクセントは地方によって違うが、沙流方言では、低から高へ上がる位置に関して著しい傾向がある。すなわち 第一音節が開音節ならば第二音節から高くなる。 sapá サパ 頭 ku=sápaha クサパハ 私の頭 第一音節が閉音節ならば第一音節が高い。 sínrit シンリッ 先祖 k=óyra コイラ 私は忘れた … この傾向に合わないとき（例外的なとき）のみ、アクセント記号を母音字の上につけて示す。 húci … k=étuhu … a=akíhi … ecioká …
tn.translation: The accent is a high-low (pitch) accent, as in Japanese. But it differs in character from the Japanese accent. In Japanese the important point is up to where the pitch is high and from where it becomes low, whereas in Ainu the point is up to where it is low and from where it becomes high. The place where it rises is fixed for each word; everything before it is low, and after it, unless raised by intonation, it usually becomes gradually lower. The accent differs by region, but in the Saru dialect there is a marked tendency regarding the position of the rise from low to high. Namely: if the first syllable is open, the pitch is high from the second syllable: sapá 'head', ku=sápaha 'my head'. …

3307.prule: Word-level intensity stress (accent d'intensité) on the initial syllable of every full (lexical) word, lexical monosyllables included; the same initial accent 'peut également se réaliser sur des mots-outils, les pronoms par exemple' ('gè-rré « nous », 'cu-ru « eux deux », p. 125), so function words are not excluded from it and, when accented, are accented initially too ('noté gèrré / noté curu' only means the regular initial mark is left unwritten, as 'kai -> noté kai); in compounds the stress falls on the initial syllable of the radical by the same rule.
3307.srule: §3.19 (p. 132, inside the 'Accent d'intensité' chapter, before the accent glottalisé section of pp. 140-142) gives the primary/secondary hierarchy of the INTENSITY accent, not of the glottal accent: in the lexically final-accented lexemes of §3.3a (p. 126: '(le signe (') indique un accent secondaire; cf. 3.19.)') 3308.heavy: Intensity scale (253), p. 185: {si, ȼhi} < Ci < CV < V(N) < CVN < (C)VV(N) ('MAYOR INTENSIDAD' to the right). 'La sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) siempre está acentuada' (p. 186); 'una sílaba CVN lleva acento cuando no está en la vecindad de una sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N)' (p. 188), i.e. long-vowel/diphthong syllables are heavy everywhere, nasal-coda syllables (the only coda type) are heavy except next to a (C)VV(N) syllable; /si/ and /ȼhi/ are extra-weak and 'casi nunca llevan acento'; word-final CV is never stressed.
3308.dflt: alternating stress from the second syllable left to right, word-final CV never stressed; primary = last assigned stress: penult in odd-parity words (hinóki, nayíri, nopóki; (259) p. 188), antepenult in even-parity words (kimítaka, hotítana, irírori; (259) p. 189); disyllables stress the first syllable (ȼíri, sári, máto, kíri, hómo; (261) p. 189) except si/ȼhi-initial disyllables before a voiceless onset, which stress the final syllable (sithá, sitó, ȼhiká, ȼhikí; (264) p. 191)
3308.prule: Weight-sensitive, word-level, fully predictable (the source: 'no es fonémico'). Ordered rules (271): (i) ACENTO DE LA SILABA FUERTE (258), p. 188: every (C)VV(N) syllable is stressed (except phrase-finally, where the stress retracts to the preceding syllable); a CVN syllable is stressed unless adjacent to a (C)VV(N) syllable. (ii) ACENTO NORMAL (262): counting from the left word edge or from a strong syllable (which 'se comporta como frontera de palabra', p. 189), alternate CV syllables are stressed starting from the second; a CV syllable immediately before a strong syllable or word-final is never stressed; disyllables stress the first syllable (261). (iii) DISLOCACION DEL ACENTO DE LA SILABA DEBIL (266), pp. 190-191: a stress due on an extra-weak si/ȼhi syllable moves to the preceding syllable; in si/ȼhi-initial disyllables the weak syllable keeps its stress before a voiced onset (the only stressed weak syllables in the language) and yields it to the final syllable before a voiceless onset (sithá, sitó, ȼhiká, ȼhikí). (iv) ACENTO PRIMARIO (268), pp. 192-193: of the stressed syllables, the last strong one ((C)VV(N) or CVN) takes primary stress if one to three CV syllables separate it from the right word edge, i.e. it lies within the last four syllables; otherwise the last assigned stress is primary (penult in odd-parity light words, antepenult in even-parity ones).
3308.srule: Every non-primary stress is secondary ('secundario o normal', [1 ACENTO], grave accent): every (C)VV(N) syllable; CVN unless adjacent to a (C)VV(N); and every second CV syllable counted left to right from the word start or from a stressed (strong) syllable, never the word-final syllable nor the syllable right before a stressed one (pokàiyapáakini, iráaWanàti, apàniróini). Optional rule (270): an extra secondary on a non-high penult in words of 4, 6, 8... normal syllables after a stressed /i/ carrying the last assigned stress (kimítaka ~ kimítàka), and on a non-high syllable after an initial strong syllable when two normal syllables follow (hóotakìri ~ hóotàkiri).

3311.prule: No placement rule. tn.translation: Akaselem, like most African languages, is a tone language, that is, the relative musical pitch of the syllables is distinctive, on the same footing as the vowels and consonants. ... Two relevant tones are distinguished in Akaselem, namely: high and low. Tone is marked in full on all vowels and syllabic nasals (that is, nasals in preconsonantal and final position). High tone is marked by an acute accent (á), and low tone by the absence of a diacritic (a).

3314.dq: there is a phonological clause stress which contrasts with phonological word stress. ... That is, a clause-final high tone syllable receives a strong stress only if it is the only high-tone syllable in the word. Otherwise it is unstressed. In cases where the final syllable of the clause is not marked by high tone, the rules for phonological word apply.
3314.heavy: Not a weight system; but within the tone-driven rules a final CLOSED high-tone syllable (type 3 CVQ, closed by glottal stop) gets light stress while other final high-tone syllables are unstressed, and the L-H penult rule applies only 'if the final syllable is an open one' (pp. 154-155).
3314.prule: Stress is not positional: every syllable carries one of two register tones (H/L) and word stress is assigned from the tone pattern by an ordered rule set with four degrees. Heavy stress on a H syllable followed by a L syllable; medium stress on the first of a run of H syllables; light stress on a final closed (glottal-stop-final) H syllable, other final H syllables unstressed; in words ending L-H with an open final syllable, light stress on the penult; L syllables otherwise unstressed. A word may carry more than one stress.
3314.srule: Tone-conditioned, graded, non-rhythmic: a word is 'marked by one or more stresses' with four degrees (heavy, medium, light, unstressed). Besides heavy stress on a H syllable before a L syllable: medium stress on the first of a series of H syllables; light stress on a word-final closed (glottal-final) H syllable, other final H syllables unstressed; light stress on the low-tone penult of a word ending L-H when the final syllable is open; L syllables otherwise unstressed. No alternating secondary stress is described.
3314.quote: A phonological word is a phonological unit consisting of one or more phonological syllables and marked by one or more stresses which are predictable from the tone pattern of the word. A high tone receives heavy stress if followed by a low-tone syllable ... The first in a series of high-tone syllables within a word receives a medium stress ...
